extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students studying discrete mathematics and proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Provide and verify solutions to standard undergraduate discrete mathematics exercises (sets, relations, functions, induction, combinatorics), using accepted proof techniques and elementary algebraic/manipulative identities. The page contains worked solutions and proof hints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by (weak) induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish a base case (usually n=1), assume the statement holds for some n, then show it holds for n+1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: for the binomial theorem and many sequence identities the text checks n=1, assumes true for n, multiplies by (x+y) and regroups to obtain the n+1 case. Show algebraic manipulation step-by-step; identify and use combinatorial coefficients when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by strong induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume the statement is true for all integers up to k (or for k or fewer sets) and then prove it for k+1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used for proofs where k+1 depends on several earlier cases (e.g., set identities with many sets, some combinatorial identities). Must include basis step(s) and explain how the hypothesis for all smaller cases yields the k+1 case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of De Morgan's laws and distributive properties in set proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Transform set expressions using De Morgan's laws, distributivity, and definitions of union/intersection/complement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show each algebraic step explicitly (e.g., {x: (x∉F) ∧ ((x∉A1) ∨ (x∉A2))} → rewrite as unions/intersections) and cite the law used. The solutions demonstrate stepwise rewriting to reach A1 ∪ A2 or similar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove inequalities by induction with algebraic manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove bounds like 1 + 1/2 + ... + 1/2^n < 2 - 1/2^n, use induction and simplify the algebra in the inductive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show base case, assume inequality for n, add next term, simplify to obtain desired bound for n+1. Keep careful control of inequalities when combining terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use recurrence relations (e.g., Fibonacci) with induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Exploit known recurrences (F_{n+2}=F_{n+1}+F_n) and perform induction to prove identities involving sums or combinations of Fibonacci numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify small n cases explicitly (often n=1,2), assume identity for k, then use recurrence to derive identity for k+1. The solutions show adding F_{k+1} to an assumed sum yields the next formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove combinatorial identities using algebraic regrouping and known binomial coefficient identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Derive formulas such as the binomial theorem by induction, using (x+y)^{n+1}=(x+y)(x+y)^n and the identity C(n,i)=C(n-1,i)+C(n-1,i-1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write out sums, change summation indices, regroup terms and apply combinatorial coefficient relations; explicitly handle edge terms (i=0 and i=n+1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting arguments using the multiplication principle
rubrics_metrics.description: When enumerating relations or functions on finite sets, count independent choices per ordered pair or per domain element, then multiply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: number of relations on A (|A|=6) is 2^{36} since each of 36 ordered pairs can be included or not. Number of functions from a 7-element set to 7-element set is 7^7; injective functions count as 7!.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show injectivity by the standard 'assume f(x)=f(y)' method
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a function is injective, assume f(x)=f(y) and manipulate algebraically to deduce x=y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrated with explicit algebra (e.g., for f(n)=2n+1 assume 2m+1=2n+1 ⇒ m=n). For rational expressions solve and ensure denominators not zero when dividing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show surjectivity by solving f(x)=b for arbitrary codomain element b
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove surjective, take arbitrary b in codomain and explicitly produce x in domain with f(x)=b, typically by algebraic inversion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the constructed x lies in the domain (and avoid illegal values such as denominators zero). Example: for f(x)=(5x+1)/(x-2) solve for x given b, check b≠5 to avoid division by zero.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate bijectivity by proving both injective and surjective (and constructing inverse)
rubrics_metrics.description: Show injective and surjective as above, then compute inverse formula when possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text exhibits inverses explicitly (e.g., inverse of f(n)=2^n is log_2). For functions given by formulas, algebraically solve for input in terms of output to get inverse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show non-injectivity or non-surjectivity by counterexample
rubrics_metrics.description: Disprove a property by providing an explicit element/pair violating it (two inputs with same image for non-injectivity; an element of codomain not hit for non-surjectivity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: f(1,0)=f(0,0) demonstrates non-injectivity; no preimage of 0 shows non-surjectivity for a sign-only valued function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the pigeonhole principle for existence statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Partition items into a finite number of classes; if more items than classes, at least two must lie in the same class leading to desired divisibility or congruence conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to remainders modulo m; e.g., among 6 integers some two share the same remainder mod 5. Use explicit partition description and count argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove relation properties (reflexive, symmetric, transitive) by direct element-chasing
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a relation has a property, take arbitrary elements and verify the defining condition using algebraic manipulation or definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give separate short proofs for reflexivity (xRx for all x), symmetry (xRy ⇒ yRx), and transitivity (xRy ∧ yRz ⇒ xRz). Use direct algebra (e.g., x-y∈Z) and simple manipulations to justify each property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe equivalence classes and partitions induced by an equivalence relation
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an equivalence relation, list or characterize equivalence classes [a]={x : xRa} and the resulting partition of the set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute representative classes explicitly (e.g., parity classes for congruence mod 2 or residue classes mod 4) and show how they partition the underlying set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct or list relations/functions explicitly as sets of ordered pairs
rubrics_metrics.description: When asked for examples, write relations/functions as explicit ordered-pair sets or by diagrams as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solutions give explicit listings for small finite sets (e.g., all relations on {a,b} or specific relations on {0,...,5}) and note properties visible from the listing (reflexive,etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove set image/preimage identities by element-wise arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Show inclusions/equalities such as f(W∩X) ⊆ f(W)∩f(X), f(W∪X)=f(W)∪f(X), f^{-1}(Y∪Z)=f^{-1}(Y)∪f^{-1}(Z), and X ⊆ f^{-1}(f(X)) using element-chasing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text demonstrates both directions of set equalities/inclusions by taking arbitrary elements and tracing membership through definitions of image and preimage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use algebraic identities among binomial coefficients (Pascal identity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply C(n,i)=C(n-1,i)+C(n-1,i-1) to regroup sums when proving the binomial theorem by induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When expanding (x+y)^{n+1} and combining sums, use the identity to identify coefficients for (x+y)^{n+1}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting injective/surjective/bijective functions between finite sets
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute counts: total functions m^n (domain size n, codomain size m), injective functions P(m,n) if m≥n, surjective counts via reasoning about images (examples shown), bijections when m=n counted by n!.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worked examples: 7^7 total functions; injective = 7!; when domain size > codomain size, injective functions are impossible; count surjective vs non-surjective examples (constant functions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove modular-relation equivalence properties using divisibility algebra
rubrics_metrics.description: For relations defined by divisibility conditions like 4|(x+3y) or 3x-5y even, prove reflexive/symmetric/transitive by manipulating integer equations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate how to rewrite expressions (multiply by constants, add equations) to show the needed divisibility for symmetry/transitivity. Then compute equivalence classes by solving congruences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove combinatorial geometry facts by induction (e.g., regions from lines)
rubrics_metrics.description: To count regions determined by n general-position lines, use induction: removing one line leaves n lines with known count, adding the line increases regions by number of intersections (n+1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show base case (one line gives 2 regions), then argue that adding the (n+1)-th line intersects previous lines in n points, dividing it into n+1 segments and creating that many new regions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derive and use explicit formulas for inverses of common bijections
rubrics_metrics.description: Given explicit bijections between sets (e.g., between Z and powers of 2, or R and (0,∞)), compute inverse maps (log_2, ln, algebraic inversion) and verify by substitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide domain restrictions where necessary and demonstrate both directions: f(f^{-1}(y))=y and f^{-1}(f(x))=x.

rubrics_metrics.name: Element-chasing with careful handling of edge cases (domains/codomain exclusions)
rubrics_metrics.description: When algebraic inversion involves division by expressions that may be zero (e.g., denominators like 5-b or x-2), explicitly note excluded values in domain/codomain and handle them in proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The solutions point out when b≠5 or x≠2 is needed to invert; always state these restrictions when proving surjectivity/injectivity or constructing inverses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of examples/counterexamples to verify or refute general claims about relations/functions
rubrics_metrics.description: To disprove statements like 'symmetric and transitive implies reflexive', provide a concrete relation on a small finite set that satisfies the premises but not the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct small relations (e.g., on {a,b,c}) showing required properties hold while reflexivity fails; explain why each property holds/fails for the example.
